bug_description.original: A vulnerability exists where attempting to open a file with a filename string starting with a NULL character is not treated the same as a zero-length string. This leads to the creation of a broken file object, causing several operations to result in a segmentation fault. Additionally, memory allocated in preparing the gs stream object is not freed in the event of such an error.
bug_description.normalized: The staged Ghostscript witness is executed as PostScript stdin by `gstoraster_fuzzer` and reaches a font-loading path that opens a filename-bearing string whose first byte is `0x00` even though its PostScript length is non-zero. `gs_parse_file_name()` accepts that string because it rejects only zero-length names; `file_prepare_stream()` then allocates a disabled stream and copies the NUL-prefixed bytes into its C-string buffer. In the vulnerable build, `file_open_stream()` notices `fname[0] == 0` and returns success immediately instead of discarding or nulling the prepared stream, so callers wrap an uninitialized stream as a readable file object. When Ghostscript later reads from that object on the same `findfont` path, the refill logic calls an unset stream `process` proc through NULL and AddressSanitizer reports a null-deref SEGV at `pc=0x0`. The fix frees the prepared stream on the `fname[0] == 0` path, sets `*ps = NULL`, and teaches `zfile()` / `zlibfile()` to convert that case into `undefinedfilename`.

source.description: First project parser step that materializes the attacker-controlled filename token as a Ghostscript file name pointer/length pair.
source.value_from: The staged 120-byte stdin witness is fed directly to Ghostscript by `gstoraster_fuzzer` (`-_`). The saved reproduction report says the PoC contains a NUL-prefixed filename token, and the bytes also contain textual PostScript tokens such as `/FontName` and `findfont`. By the time `gs_parse_file_name()` runs, Ghostscript has a PostScript string whose explicit `len` is non-zero even though `pname[0] == 0`.

sink.description: Source-grounded sink that explains the saved null-PC crash: the first refill on the broken file object dispatches through an unset stream `process` proc.
sink.note: The saved ASan trace has no symbolized project frame, only `pc=0x0`, `address=0x0`, and `READ`. This line is the concrete NULL function-pointer call on the witnessed `findfont`/`read` path after `file_open_stream()` returns a disabled stream as if the open succeeded.

root_cause.description: The common file opener treats a NUL-prefixed filename as a successful no-op and leaves the partially prepared stream pointer live instead of discarding it or returning an error/NULL.
root_cause.note: Immediately before this branch, `file_prepare_stream()` has already allocated `*ps` and populated its buffer with the NUL-prefixed filename bytes. The vulnerable early return skips both cleanup and `file_init_stream()`, so later code receives an uninitialized stream that still carries a valid-looking `read_id`. The fix frees the buffer and stream, sets `*ps = NULL`, and relies on callers to reject that case as `undefinedfilename`.

parser_admitted.description: The fuzz target feeds the witness to Ghostscript as PostScript stdin, and the textual witness reaches the built-in `findfont` procedure during page 1 rendering. That enters the font-loading path that later opens the filename-bearing object and performs the crashing read.

tainted_value_origin.description: The tainted value is the filename string viewed in Ghostscript's length-tracked representation: positive `len`, but first byte `0x00`. Later code reuses both fields and eventually reinterprets the same bytes as an empty C string.

coarse_trace.summary: The harness feeds the 120-byte witness to Ghostscript as stdin (`-_`) and starts rendering page 1.
Ghostscript parses the attacker-controlled PostScript filename token into a `fname` pointer and explicit length and accepts it because only zero-length names are rejected.
The common file opener allocates a stream for that filename, then returns success on `fname[0] == 0` without initializing or discarding the stream.
The `findfont` path reads from the returned file object while scanning the font header, and the broken stream reaches Ghostscript's low-level refill path.
The refill logic dispatches through a NULL stream `process` proc and matches the saved null-deref SEGV at `pc=0x0`.

fine_trace.note: Ghostscript performs its only emptiness check on `len == 0`. Because the witness filename token has a non-zero PostScript length, the no-device path preserves the raw pointer and explicit length even though the first byte is `0x00`, so the NUL-prefixed name is treated as a real filename.

Allocates a new stream and backing buffer, copies the attacker-controlled filename bytes into that buffer, appends a C terminator, and publishes the stream via `*ps`. Because `file_alloc_stream()` leaves a newly allocated stream disabled until `file_init_stream()` runs, the copied object is only partially prepared at this point. With `fname[0] == 0`, the C-string view in `buffer` is immediately empty even though the tracked PostScript length from step 1 was non-zero.

Takes the NUL-prefixed filename branch and reports success. The code does not free the buffer from step 2, does not null `*ps`, and does not call `file_init_stream()`, so the caller receives a live pointer to a stream that still lacks the read/seek/process machinery of a real file stream.

Wraps the still-disabled stream in a readable PostScript file object. `file_alloc_stream()` initialized `s->read_id` before the failed open, and this function stores that same ID into the file reference, so later `read` validation sees an apparently valid open file even though `file_init_stream()` never ran.

On the witness `findfont` path, Ghostscript begins scanning the opened font/resource file by issuing `read` on the returned file object. The staged witness is textual PostScript, not TTF/OTF/WOFF magic, so the non-TTF `.findfontvalue` helper is the applicable first consumer of that file object.

The `read` operator accepts the broken file object because `check_read_file` only compares the file reference's stored size with `s->read_id`. It does not verify that an OS file was actually opened or that `file_init_stream()` installed read procs.

The first refill on the accepted file object reaches `sreadbuf()`. Because the stream from steps 2-4 never passed through `file_init_stream()`, `curr->procs.process` was never installed; the dispatch goes through NULL, which matches the saved `pc=0x0`, `READ`, and `AddressSanitizer: SEGV` with no symbolized stack.

sanitizer_ground_truth.source: parsed from staged reproduction_report.json and sanitizer_trace.txt

cross_validation.sink_matches_crash: Partially. AddressSanitizer only reported `pc=0x0` / `<unknown module>`, but fine-trace step 7 is the concrete NULL function-pointer call on the same source-grounded `findfont` read path and is the first project sink that explains a zero-page read after the broken file object is consumed.
cross_validation.trace_consistent_with_stack: Partially. The saved crash trace contains no symbolized project frames, only page-rendering progress and the final null-PC SEGV. The staged witness bytes, Ghostscript's PostScript font loader, and the vulnerable stream code are consistent with the reconstructed path `findfont -> read -> zread -> sreadbuf`.
cross_validation.tainted_value_reaches_sink: Yes. The NUL-prefixed filename survives `gs_parse_file_name()`, is copied into a newly allocated stream buffer, triggers the vulnerable `fname[0] == 0` success return in `file_open_stream()`, is wrapped as a readable file object by `make_stream_file()`, and is then consumed by the font loader's first `read`, which forces `sreadbuf()` to dispatch through a null `procs.process` pointer.

format.name: Ghostscript/PostScript stdin document with a NUL-prefixed filename token
format.contract: The witness must be a Ghostscript stdin document whose relevant filename string has a non-zero PostScript length but begins with byte `0x00`. In the staged witness that textual input also reaches `findfont`, so Ghostscript opens that filename on the font-loading path and then reads from the broken file object created by the vulnerable `fname[0] == 0` success return.
